title: UK weather forecast: Will there be another heatwave in September? - The Independent
search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Assam
full_text:
The Met Office has issued thunderstorm warnings across parts of the UK, warning there is a “small risk of flooding and disruption” after a record-breaking summer.
Yellow storm warnings will come into force for the West and East Midlands, as well as the North West, South East, South West and east of England, and parts of Wales.
An alert will be in place from 3am until 10pm on Wednesday, and from 6am until 10pm on Thursday.
It comes after back-to-back heatwaves left the ground hard and dry, with 70 per cent of England and Wales in drought.
Provisional Met Office data shows that the UK’s mean temperature for meteorological summer so far is currently at 16.48C – that is 1.88C above the 1991 to 2020 average temperature. England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average.
The remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.
But will there be another dry and sunny spell?
What does the long range forecast say?
Looking ahead, the Met Office’s long range weather forecast predicts that “an unsettled period is likely” heading into September, with the amount of rainfall likely to “be above average for the time year”.
However, the forecaster notes that “some drier and more settled interludes could develop at times”, and while “temperatures are likely to be near average... some short-lived warm or very warm spells are possible, especially in the south.”
Moving further into the month, the forecaster predicts that “drier weather may become more prevalent, especially in the south and southeast, with any more unsettled conditions tending to become more likely further north and northwest”.
It adds: “Temperatures will probably be near normal at first but may become warmer later, with the possibility of some hot spells in the south.”
What records have been broken this summer?
The Met Office said earlier this month that temperatures had reached 37.6C at Charlwood in Surrey, while at Wisley temperatures had hit 37.2C, and Kew Gardens in London had recorded a temperature of 38.1C – the highest temperature recorded in the UK this year.
A further 10 weather stations were at or above 36C, the provisional figures from the Met Office showed.
It makes 2026 the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold.
Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.
It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.
For four months in a row temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.
July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.
By 15 July this year the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.
Why is the UK experiencing more heatwaves?
Climate change is making extremes such as heat and drought more intense and more likely.
The UK's weather is becoming warmer and wetter, and adverse weather events - heatwaves, flooding, extreme cold - are growing more frequent and intense. The last decade has been warmer than any previous decade on record, and summers we once considered exceptional are becoming the norm.
The Met Office explains that the UK is experiencing higher maximum temperatures and longer warm spells in recent years. Warm spells have seen their average length more than double – increasing from 5.3 days in 1961-90 to over 13 days in the decade 2008-2017.
But the outlook could get worse. A study by the Met Office Hadley Centre suggests the current chance of seeing days reaching 40C or more is extremely low. However, by 2100 under a high emissions scenario the UK could see 40 C days every three to four years.

title: Extreme heat costs Bangladesh $4.1 billion in lost wages each year: Study - Down To Earth
search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Assam
full_text:
Extreme heat is taking a significant toll on the incomes, health and livelihoods of Bangladesh’s informal workers, according to new study by the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED), an independent research organisation and Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program, a community based migrant workers’ organisation in Bangladesh.
The study highlights how rising temperatures are reducing productivity, cutting wages and increasing health risks among workers who often have limited access to social protection.
The study selected Dhaka for its high exposure to extreme heat, large informal workforce and the presence of grassroots organisations and worker groups that could help researchers reach vulnerable workers.
Using the Comprehensive Climate Impact Quantification toolkit, the researchers interviewed 175 informal work households in Dhaka, including outdoor workers involved in construction and rickshaw pulling and indoor workers employed in garment manufacturing.
Informal workers account for 84.9 per cent of Bangladesh’s workforce, making heat exposure a major economic and social concern.
Heat reducing productivity, incomes
Heat is imposing measurable economic losses. Outdoor workers lose an average of 23.7 workdays each year due to heat, compared with 13.5 days among indoor workers. Illness was the largest contributor, accounting for 15.3 lost days among outdoor workers and 8.1 among indoor workers, followed by reduced productivity.
These losses translate into annual wage losses of $148.86 per outdoor worker and $89.10 per indoor worker. For low-income households, such losses can force families to borrow money, reduce food consumption and delayed healthcare.
Heat creating serious health risks
Heat exposure is also creating serious health risks. Workers reported heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heatstroke. According to the study, around one in three outdoor and one in seven indoor workers reach the threshold for heatstroke, which is a medical emergency. Repeated dehydration is a particular concern. The study found that 23.1 per cent of workers showed symptoms consistent with acute kidney injury, and around 6 per cent, or one in 17 workers, may eventually develop chronic kidney disease from repeated heat exposure.
The effects extend to mental health. Psychological stress reportedly doubled during the hot season, with workers experiencing low mood, anxiety, irritability, workplace mistakes and sleep difficulties.
Heat deepening poverty, widening living wage deficit
The study found that heatwaves are deepening poverty. Heat is also widening the gap between household earnings and Dhaka’s living wage, estimated at about $2,997 annually. Outdoor-worker households earn an average of $1,756, while indoor-worker households earn $1,985. After heat-related wage losses, annual household income falls to $1,607 and $1,896, respectively.
The national economic costs are substantial. IIED estimates that extreme heat causes about $4.1 billion in wage losses across Bangladesh each year, equivalent to 0.91 per cent of GDP. Heat-related chronic kidney disease could add another $2.12 billion in losses.
Strengthening protections
The researchers recommend strengthening social protection through weather-triggered cash transfers delivered via bKash and Nagad and targeted through the National Identity system. Seasonal mobile health camps are also proposed because existing government health schemes do not currently reach urban informal workers.
The study calls for stronger workplace protections. Bangladesh’s labour laws currently lack a binding temperature threshold for safe work and do not recognise heatstroke or heat-related kidney disease as occupational illnesses eligible for compensation.
The study recommends an enforceable heat threshold, with mandatory drinking water, shade and rest breaks once it is crossed; recognition of heat-related illness as an occupational disease and protection for every worker exposed to hazardous heat, regardless of the size of the establishment.
